summary.text: Capillary action is a liquid flowing in a narrow space without help from outside forces such as gravity.
In a tube of small enough diameter, surface tension from cohesion in the liquid and adhesion between the liquid and the wall act to propel the liquid.
It shows up in paper towels, sponges, wicking fabrics and fountain pens, which draw ink to the nib.

items.prompt: The corner of a paper towel touches a spill, and the liquid creeps into the towel. What lets it move?

options.label: The towel pulls it in like a vacuum, using suction from the air
Gravity drags it down into the towel's thickness
It flows through tiny spaces without needing gravity or another outside force
The towel heats the liquid until it flows inward

items.explain: Capillary action is a liquid flowing in a narrow space, such as the pores of paper, without help from external forces like gravity.

items.prompt: Two glass tubes, one narrow and one wide, stand in water. Which pulls a column of water up further?

options.label: The narrow one
The wide one, because it holds more water
Neither, because gravity treats both columns the same
The wide one, because there is more wall to cling to

items.explain: The contact length grows with the radius, but the column's weight grows with the radius squared, so a narrow tube draws a liquid column along further.

items.prompt: Mercury sits in a glass tube. Its molecules attract each other more strongly than they attract the glass. What does the mercury do?

options.label: Its surface curves inward and it rises higher than water would
It rises exactly like water, since glass is the same
It sticks to the wall and refuses to move at all
Its surface curves outward and it is not drawn up the tube

items.explain: When the forces within the liquid exceed those between solid and liquid, as with mercury and glass, a convex meniscus forms and capillary action works in reverse.

items.prompt: In the 1600s Boyle put a tube of red wine in a partial vacuum, and the wine's height in the capillary did not change. What did he conclude?

options.label: Air pressure pushes the liquid up the tube
Liquids in these tubes behave differently from mercury in barometers
Red wine is special, and plain water would have dropped
The vacuum was too weak to show any effect

items.explain: The vacuum had no observable influence on the height, so the behavior of liquids in capillary tubes was due to a different phenomenon from that governing mercury barometers.

items.prompt: A garden has one soggy patch next to a bone-dry patch. What moves groundwater from the wet area toward the dry one?

options.label: Gravity alone, pulling water sideways through the soil
The dry soil, which sucks water in the way a vacuum would
Attraction of water molecules to soil particles, driven by differences in soil potential
Evaporation, which pushes water horizontally

items.explain: Capillary action describes the attraction of water molecules to soil particles and moves groundwater from wet to dry areas, driven by differences in soil potential.

items.prompt: You set up a wet cotton cord to carry water from one container to another. Where must the full container sit?

options.label: Higher than the receiving container
Lower than the receiving container
At exactly the same height as the receiving container
It does not matter, since the cord pulls either way

items.explain: In a capillary action siphon, a saturated cord runs from a reservoir to a receiving vessel, and the reservoir must be higher.

paragraphs.heading: Liquid that moves itself
paragraphs.text: Capillary action is a liquid travelling through a narrow space on its own, with no help from an outside force such as gravity. It also goes by names like capillarity, capillary rise and wicking. You can watch it as liquid climbs between the hairs of a paint brush, up a thin straw, or into porous materials such as paper and plaster. The name comes from the Latin capillaris, meaning like a hair, because a capillary has a tiny diameter, as thin as a hair.

paragraphs.heading: The forces behind it
paragraphs.text: The cause is the pull between molecules of the liquid and the surfaces around it. Two pulls work together. One is surface tension, which comes from cohesion inside the liquid; the other is adhesion between the liquid and the wall of its container. When a tube is narrow enough, the pair drive the liquid along. Adhesion drags the column up the inner wall until there is enough liquid for its weight, pulled by gravity, to win.

paragraphs.heading: Why narrow tubes pull higher
paragraphs.text: Put the bottom of a glass tube in water and the surface inside forms a curve called a concave meniscus. The rim where the top of the column touches the tube grows in step with the tube's radius. The weight of the column, though, grows with the square of the radius. So a narrow tube can lift liquid further than a wide one, as long as the molecules in the middle hold on well enough to those at the edge.

paragraphs.heading: When it runs backwards
paragraphs.text: Liquids do not always climb. With some pairs, such as mercury and glass, the liquid pulls on itself more strongly than it pulls on the solid. The surface then bulges into a convex meniscus, and capillary action works in reverse.

paragraphs.heading: From Leonardo to Einstein
paragraphs.text: Leonardo da Vinci made the first recorded observation of the effect. In 1660 the Irish chemist Robert Boyle still treated it as a novelty. He dipped a thin tube in red wine and put it under a partial vacuum, and the wine's height did not visibly change, so he decided something other than what drives a mercury barometer was at work. A successful mathematical account arrived in 1805, when Thomas Young in Britain and Pierre-Simon Laplace in France derived the Young–Laplace equation. Albert Einstein's first paper, submitted in 1900, was on capillarity.

paragraphs.heading: In towels, pens and eyes
paragraphs.text: Paper towels and sponges soak up spills this way, and the small pores of a sponge behave like tiny capillaries. Some fabrics are said to wick sweat away from the skin, named after the wicks of candles and lamps. A fountain pen uses the effect to draw ink from its cartridge or reservoir to the tip of the nib. In your own body, it drains the tear fluid that your eyes produce all the time.

paragraphs.heading: In soil and walls
paragraphs.text: In the ground, capillary action moves water from wet parts of the soil to dry parts. In buildings, the same effect lies behind rising damp in concrete and masonry. One handy use is the capillary siphon: a soaked cotton cord runs from a raised reservoir of water down into a lower vessel, with no hollow tube needed.
